extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning calculus and rigorous proofs (limits, continuity, sequences, series)
extracted.subtask_description: Proving limits, continuity, convergence/divergence using epsilon-delta/N definitions and standard limit/sequence/series theorems; includes constructive strategies (choose δ/N), limit laws, and divergence tests. Geared toward writing rigorous textbook-style proofs in a first/second-semester calculus or introduction-to-proof course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epsilon–delta definition of limit (Definition 13.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a function f and a number c, lim_{x->c} f(x) = L means: for any ε > 0 there is a δ > 0 such that 0 < |x - c| < δ implies |f(x) - L| < ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the foundational criterion for proving limits: given an arbitrary ε>0, construct a δ (often as an explicit function of ε, or the minimum of several constraints) so that 0<|x-c|<δ implies the desired bound. Examples show choosing δ = ε, δ = ε/3, or δ = min{1, ε/5} depending on algebraic manipulations. Use this definition both for direct proofs and for contradiction proofs that assume a limit exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two ways a limit can fail / contradiction method
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting statement lim_{x->c} f(x)=L can be false either because there exists a different number M ≠ L with lim_{x->c} f(x)=M, or because Statement (13.4) is false for all L∈R. Contradiction is one way to prove that lim f(x) does not exist: assume lim f(x)=L and produce a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show nonexistence, assume a candidate limit L exists and derive conflicting bounds (often by choosing two sequences or points approaching c from different sides yielding function values far apart). Example: pick points a and b on either side of c to force |f(b)-f(a)| to exceed the sum of two small ε-bounds, reaching a contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounding auxiliary x-dependent factors by restricting δ
rubrics_metrics.description: When |f(x)-L| factors include expressions like |x+2| that depend on x, first choose δ small enough (e.g., δ<1) so that x is close to c and the companion factor is bounded (e.g., |x+2|<5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common pattern in ε–δ proofs: isolate a factor of |x-c| and bound the remaining x-dependent factor by choosing δ ≤ 1 (or another convenient small constant). Then obtain |f(x)-L| ≤ (constant)·|x-c| and choose δ accordingly (e.g., δ ≤ min{1, ε/(constant)}). The textbook illustrates this with |5x^2 - 20| where |x+2| is bounded by 5 when |x-2|<1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of basic inequalities (triangle-type bounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inequalities (13.1)-(13.3): for any x,y∈R, |x - y| ≤ |x| + |y|, ||x| - |y|| ≤ |x - y|, and | |x| - |y| | ≤ |x - y| (variants used frequently).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elementary inequalities are used freely to split |f(x)-L| into sums of simpler terms and to bound differences. Proofs of limit laws and many manipulations rely on replacing |A+B| by ≤ |A| + |B| and similar triangle-inequality manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Min/combination-of-deltas strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving statements that require multiple existing δ-values (e.g., from separate limits), take δ = min{δ_1, δ_2, ...} to satisfy all constraints simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard construction when combining limits (sum, product, composition): for given ε choose how to split ε among parts or pick δ_i for each part, then let δ be the minimum so all parts' conditions hold. Example: in the sum rule choose δ = min{δ', δ''} coming from the two limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constant function and identity limit rules (Theorems 13.2 & 13.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constant function rule: if f(x)=a then lim_{x->c} a = a. Identity function rule: lim_{x->c} x = c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs are trivial by the ε–δ definition: for constants the difference is zero; for the identity take δ = ε. These serve as base cases or building blocks when proving limits of polynomials etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constant multiple rule (Theorem 13.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If lim_{x->c} f(x) exists and a∈R, then lim_{x->c} a f(x) = a·lim_{x->c} f(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use algebra |a f(x) - aL| = |a| · |f(x)-L| and the existing δ for f to control |f(x)-L|; pick same δ. Handle trivial a=0 separately if desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum and difference rules (Theorems 13.5 & 13.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If lim f(x) and lim g(x) exist, then lim (f+g) = lim f + lim g, and lim (f - g) = lim f - lim g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Split |(f+g) - (L+M)| ≤ |f-L| + |g-M|, pick δ's for f and g from their limits, then δ=min{δ_f, δ_g}. Difference rule follows from sum and constant multiple rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication rule and strategy to bound |g(x)| (Theorem 13.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If lim f(x)=L and lim g(x)=M exist, then lim f g = LM. Key issue: a factor |g(x)| can grow while |f(x)-L| shrinks, so bound |g(x)| by making |g(x)-M| small (e.g., <1) to get |g(x)| < 1+|M|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof technique: choose δ' so |g(x)-M|<1 (hence |g(x)| ≤ 1+|M|), and choose δ'' to make |f(x)-L| small; then use triangle/inequality manipulations to obtain |f g - LM| ≤ (1+|M|)|f-L| + |L|·|g-M| and make each term < ε/2 by appropriate δ choices; finally let δ=min{δ',δ''...}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division rule and avoiding zero denominator (Theorem 13.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If lim f(x)=L and lim g(x)=M with M ≠ 0, then lim f/g = L/M. Must ensure g(x) is bounded away from zero near c so division is valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose δ' so that |g(x)-M| < |M|/2 (or similar), which implies |g(x)| > |M|/2, so 1/|g(x)| is bounded. Then bound |f/g - L/M| by splitting into terms and making them small via δ choices; take δ as minimum of the constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition rule (Theorem 13.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If lim_{x->c} g(x) = L and f is continuous at L, then lim_{x->c} f(g(x)) = f(L).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given ε>0, use continuity of f at L to get a δ' for f, then use the limit of g to get δ so |g(x)-L|<δ' when 0<|x-c|<δ; conclude |f(g(x))-f(L)|<ε. This highlights that continuity of outer function is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity at a point (Definition 13.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: f is continuous at x=c if lim_{x->c} f(x) = f(c). Equivalently, three conditions must hold: (1) f(c) is defined, (2) lim_{x->c} f(x) exists, (3) lim_{x->c} f(x) = f(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove continuity use the ε–δ definition of the limit and show the limit equals the function value. Many familiar functions (polynomials, rational functions where denominator nonzero) are continuous on their domains; continuity underpins composition and other limit rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiability implies continuity (Theorem 13.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is differentiable at c (i.e., the limit defining f'(c) exists), then f is continuous at c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof rewrites f(x) = f'(c)·(x-c) + f(c) and uses limit laws to see lim_{x->c} f(x) = f(c). This is a standard fact to justify continuity when using derivative assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit at infinity definition (Definition 13.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: lim_{x->∞} f(x) = L means: for any ε>0 there exists N>0 such that x>N implies |f(x)-L|<ε. Analogously for x->-∞ with N<0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use N instead of δ: given ε construct N (often via inequalities/bounds). Example: to show sin(x)/x -> 0, use -1 ≤ sin x ≤ 1 to get |sin x / x| ≤ 1/x and choose N > 1/ε.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergence to ±∞ (limits at infinity that are infinite)
rubrics_metrics.description: lim_{x->∞} f(x) = +∞ means for any real L there exists N such that x>N implies f(x) > L. Similarly for -∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to formalize statements like lim x^2 = ∞. Proofs use contradiction with the ε/N framework: assume finite limit, get contradiction via choosing sufficiently large x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence convergence (Definition 13.5) and proof pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence {a_n} converges to L if for any ε>0 there exists N∈N such that n > N implies |a_n - L| < ε. For sequences, choose an explicit N (often as a function of ε) to control terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs parallel function limits at infinity: pick N to make tail terms small. Typical strategies include algebraic bounds relating n and a_n; examples show choosing N so that 1/N < ε, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series convergence via partial sums (Definition 13.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: A series ∑ a_k converges to S if the sequence of partial sums s_n = ∑_{k=1}^n a_k converges to S. If {s_n} diverges, the series diverges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove convergence, analyze s_n and use sequence convergence tests. Example: geometric series formula for s_n yields closed form whose limit is computed. Many practical convergence tests (comparison, ratio, root, alternating) are used instead of direct ε–N proofs, but can be justified from these definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergence test for series (Theorem 13.11 & Corollary 13.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ∑ a_k converges then a_k -> 0. Contrapositive (divergence test): if a_k does not converge to 0 (or converges to nonzero), then ∑ a_k diverges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To use the test: compute or inspect lim a_k; if it's not 0, immediately conclude series diverges. The theorem's proof uses partial sums: a_n = s_n - s_{n-1} and the convergence of s_n implies a_n -> 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard strategies for proving nonexistence of a limit via sequences/side-limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce two sequences (or points) approaching c for which f(x) tends to different numbers (or diverges). This shows the limit does not exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: piecewise functions where left-hand and right-hand expressions give different values; trig oscillations like sin(1/x) where function values oscillate arbitrarily near 0. Use ε=some value (e.g., 1/2) and pick appropriate sequence terms to contradict the ε–δ condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of min/explicit choices and splitting ε among terms
rubrics_metrics.description: When error |f(x)-L| is split into several terms, decide how to allocate the total ε to each term (e.g., make each < ε/2 or ε/3) and pick δ/N accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in proofs of product, sum, division rules: split target ε into pieces, find δ_i to make each contribution small, then take δ = min{δ_i}. The textbook repeatedly uses choices like make each term < ε/2 or ε/3 and then combine by triangle inequality.
